# Browser Automation Basics (Selenium and Playwright)

## Overview
Sometimes an app has no API and no integration - you can only use it through its website - and that is exactly when browser automation saves the day by controlling a real browser the way a human would. Tools like Selenium and Playwright launch Chrome or Firefox programmatically and can navigate to pages, fill forms, click buttons, and read content, letting you automate tasks on sites that offer no other way in (legacy portals, internal tools, sites without APIs). Playwright is the more modern, faster, and reliable choice and is worth favoring, though Selenium is older and very widely used. The core skill is locating elements: you tell the tool which button or field to act on using selectors (by ID, CSS selector, text, or role), so understanding a bit of how web pages are structured helps. Once you can find elements, you drive the page - type into inputs, click, select from dropdowns, and navigate between pages. A key beginner lesson is waiting: pages load asynchronously, so your script must wait for elements to appear rather than acting too soon, which is the number-one cause of flaky browser automations; Playwright's auto-waiting makes this easier. You will also learn headless mode (running the browser invisibly in the background, ideal for servers). Importantly, browser automation is powerful but more fragile than APIs - it breaks when the site's layout changes and can be slower - so the professional judgment is to prefer APIs when they exist and use browser automation only when there is no better option. Knowing this technique dramatically widens the range of tasks you can automate.

## Deep Dive
This module covers: What browser automation is and when to use it; Selenium and Playwright overview; Locating elements (selectors); Clicking, typing, and navigating; Waiting, reliability, and headless mode. Mastering these ideas is essential because they appear repeatedly in production AI systems.

### What You Will Learn
- The core theory behind today's topic.
- How to apply it using Python, NumPy, Pandas, or the relevant framework.
- How to evaluate results and avoid common mistakes.
- Where to find authoritative references when you need deeper detail.

### Real-World Context
In industry, these skills are used daily: data scientists clean messy survey data, AI engineers deploy models to REST APIs, and automation engineers orchestrate pipelines. Today's practical task simulates one of these real-world scenarios.

## Hands-On Practice
Practical Task: Install Playwright (or Selenium) and write a script that opens a website, fills in a search box, submits it, waits for results, and extracts the first few result titles.
Mini Project: Automate a repetitive web task end to end: log into a demo site (or use a public form), navigate to a page, enter data, submit, capture a confirmation, and save the result - with proper waits so it runs reliably.
Assignment: Explain when you would choose browser automation over an API, list two reasons browser automation is more fragile, and describe how waiting prevents flaky scripts.

Complete all three sections. Each completed section earns points toward your CalibiAI Score. If you are unsure about any part, use the AI assessment popup to submit your work and receive dynamic feedback from DeepSeek.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid
Many beginners rush into coding before fully understanding the data. Others skip validation steps and overestimate model performance. This module helps you build the discipline of checking assumptions first, then applying algorithms systematically.

## Career Impact
The skills covered today are frequently tested in technical interviews and required in entry-level AI engineering roles. Building a portfolio that demonstrates mastery of these concepts will significantly improve your job prospects.

## Key Takeaways
1. Theory guides practice — understand before coding.
2. Clean data and clear metrics are more valuable than complex models.
3. Document your steps for reproducibility.
4. Communication matters: explain results to non-technical stakeholders.
